The Women Who Glowed in the Dark
The Company That Knew the Paint Was Killing Them
description: In the 1910s and 1920s, hundreds of young women were hired to paint watch dials with glowing radium paint. The company told them it was safe. It was not. This is the true story of the Radium Girls — and the executives who watched them die.

summary_short.hook: They told the girls to lick the brushes
summary_short.say: In the 1920s, young women were paid to paint glowing watch dials with radium. The company told them the paint was harmless. So they pointed the brushes with their lips. Within a few years their jaws began to crumble. Their bones glowed. The company already knew the paint was deadly. They kept the girls working anyway. This is the story of the Radium Girls. The full story is on the channel.

facts_to_check: US Radium Corporation hired young women to paint dials with radium-226 paint starting around 1917
Workers were instructed to shape the brush tip with their lips ('lip-pointing')
Company scientists and managers handled the paint with protection while the painters did not
Grace Fryer was diagnosed with radium poisoning and sued in the mid-1920s
Catherine Donohue's case in Illinois became a major public fight in the 1930s
Many of the women developed 'radium jaw' — necrosis of the jawbone
The paint was luminous because of radium; the girls' clothes and skin would glow
Internal company knowledge of the danger existed years before the public lawsuits
Settlements were reached; several of the original plaintiffs died young from radiation-related disease
The cases helped push later occupational safety standards in the United States

scenes.say: They told the girls to point the brushes with their lips. It made the tips finer. The paint tasted like chalk. At night, some of them noticed their clothes still glowed.
This is the story of the Radium Girls. Young women hired to paint the numbers on watches and instruments so soldiers and civilians could read them in the dark.

scenes.say: The paint was called Undark. It contained radium-226. The company that made it was the United States Radium Corporation, based in Orange, New Jersey.

scenes.say: Most of the painters were teenagers or women in their early twenties. The work paid better than many factory jobs. They were told the paint was safe.

scenes.say: While the girls lip-pointed the brushes, the company’s own chemists and managers handled the same material with gloves, screens, and caution. That difference mattered.
By the mid-1920s, some of the women began to suffer severe dental problems. Teeth fell out. Jaws became infected and crumbled. Doctors had never seen anything quite like it.
Grace Fryer was one of the first to fight back. She had worked at the Orange plant. When she became ill, she tried to sue the company. Finding a lawyer who would take the case was difficult.
The company denied responsibility. They suggested the women’s illnesses came from poor hygiene or syphilis. Internal knowledge of radium’s dangers already existed inside the industry.
In Illinois, another group of dial painters, including Catherine Donohue, faced the same slow poisoning. Her case became public and ugly. She testified while severely ill.
Medical examinations showed radioactive material deposited in their bones. The body treated radium like calcium. Once it was inside, it stayed there, irradiating the marrow and the bone for years.

Several of the original New Jersey plaintiffs reached a settlement in 1928. It was not large by modern standards. Many of them died within a few years from cancers and blood diseases linked to the exposure.

scenes.say: Catherine Donohue died in 1938. Her death, and the public fight around it, helped force attention onto industrial radiation hazards in the United States.

scenes.say: The Radium Girls did not set out to become symbols. They took a factory job that paid better than most. The company had more information than they did. That imbalance killed them.
Their cases helped build the argument that employers owe workers honest information about invisible dangers. That argument is still being fought in different industries today.
